name: Nair depilatory

lead: Nair is a long-running chemical hair remover, launched in 1940 and now owned by Church & Dwight. It is sold in women's and men's lines.
It is a temporary method: the follicle is left intact so hair grows back.

paras: Thioglycolate or calcium hydroxide breaks keratin's disulfide bonds so the hair can be wiped off.
Harsh actives can irritate skin; no brand-specific clinical studies were found.

lead: Nair is an American brand of chemical depilatory products, including creams, lotions and sprays, that remove hair by breaking down keratin so it can be wiped from the skin. According to Wikipedia, the original lotion launched in 1940 and the brand is now owned by Church & Dwight, which bought it from Carter-Wallace in 2001.[1]

The name is described as a portmanteau of "no hair." Its depilatories use calcium hydroxide and, in some formulas, potassium thioglycolate to break the disulfide bonds in hair keratin, with softening agents such as mineral oil added to offset the harshness of the actives.[1] The depilatory category in general leaves the dermal papilla intact, so hair regrows.[2]
No clinical studies specific to the brand were found.

paras: The original Nair lotion launched in 1940. A television campaign built on a 1958 song, "We wear short shorts," won a Clio Award; in 2001 a men's line was added, and by 2007 the brand sold about 25 products including waxes and bleaches.[1]
Depilatory creams typically contain thioglycolate salts at a few percent in a base with a pH near 12; hair breakdown takes about ten minutes, after which the product is rinsed off.[2]

Neither source gives clinical safety data for Nair. Wikipedia notes only that the active ingredients are harsh, which is why softening agents are included.[1] Product labels commonly advise patch testing and limits on application time; these are manufacturer instructions.

timeline.event: Church & Dwight acquires Nair; men's line introduced.[1]
